messages.body_plain: Thanks for the feedback! The problem is not about child documents, but the chunk option fig.align='center' in your child documents. This option is not really for the "general-purpose" Markdown, because Markdown does not support the alignment of images. What knitr does when it sees fig.align in Markdown is to generate HTML code instead of using the original Markdown syntax ![]() to write images. At the moment, Pandoc does not seem to recognize the tag when it converts Markdown to LaTeX. I think we will solve this problem in the future by using native LaTeX code to write figures when the document output is expected to be PDF. For now, the best strategy is to avoid anything that is not supported in the native (Pandoc) Markdown syntax. Taking a look at the knitr plot hook shows that an extra newline is not generated before the image tag is placed in the generated markdown, which makes complete sense as knitr shouldn't be placing extra line endings in documents. This is exactly the type of situation that knitLiteral was made for; displaying what is literally required to get the intended result without breaking the single point of trouble principle. plot(1:2,1:2)

On 4/24/2014 10:22 PM, Yihui Xie wrote:
> spin() also saves graphics to files, so what did I miss here? knitr

I will try to argue the use case here, as it is similar to one way in
which I use knitr.

One purpose of an R script can be the creation of an artifact. For
example, the script may import some data, clean it, apply some model to
it, and create a plot of some combination of the data and the model.
This plot is to be used elsewhere (figure in a manuscript, slide in a
presentation, printed in large format and used as a billboard, etc.). It
is useful to have a script so that the process of creating the plot is
fully documented and automated.

Along comes spin, and now there is an easy way to create a second
artifact: a pretty-ish version of all the steps that were taken to
create the plot. While this second artifact includes the generated plot
as well, its existence does not remove the requirement of creating the
first artifact (the saved graphics file).

Now, scripts can be far more complicated than this, but it is still
reasonable that a script should save a graphics file (with specific
characteristics such as size and type) for further use elsewhere in
addition to displaying the graphic in the document itself.

I've discussed this in terms of using spin on a script, but the argument
is really the same for knitting with any of the hybrid formats (.Rmd,
.Rnw). Sometimes you need to save a graphics file for use outside the
R/knitr ecosystem. Explicit use of ggsave (for example) is proper in
these cases.

I do agree that manually saving a plot just to manually insert it in the
document you are creating is not an efficient way to do things and
should generally be discouraged. But there are reasons to generate a
plot other than to just display it in the document being created by knitr.

--Brian Diggs

Not to sound flippant, but what do you mean by "right place"? I assume
you mean right where the code chunk is. However, LaTeX, by default would
not agree with that. One of the features of LaTeX is the ability to have
"floating" figures. Rather than appearing exactly where they are
included, a float (figure, table, etc.) can float to somewhere else such
as the bottom of the page, the top of the next page, or on a page by
itself. Without a caption, figures are not put inside a figure
environment (which is a floating environment) and so appear exactly
where the code chunk is. But adding a caption triggers them being put
inside a figure (floating) environment and thus going where LaTeX things
is best. You can add the chunk option `fig.pos = "H"` which tells LaTeX
that the best place is right here and nowhere else. This also requires
including the LaTeX package float (add `\usepackage{float}` to the
document preamble.

> Thanks

--Brian Diggs
